slides.title: Sensors in Robotics
slides.text:
Sensors in Robotics
•  Robot sensors are devices that enable robots to perceive,
  measure, and interact with their environment or internal state,
  mimicking human senses like sight, hearing, and touch.
•  In robotics, sensors act as the eyes, ears, and skin of the system by
   collecting real-time information about physical conditions such as
   distance, position, motion, light, and orientation.
•  Without sensors, a robot cannot make intelligent
   decisions or operate autonomously.





                                                                                                           3

visualInspection.notes: All three bullets viewed. Sensors observe environment or internal state and deliver physical-condition information. The absolute claim that robots cannot operate autonomously without sensors needs a bounded interpretation: open-loop programmed behavior can exist, but adaptation to unobserved changes is unsupported.

slides.title: Role of Sensors in a Robotic System
slides.text:
Role of Sensors in a Robotic System

•  Convert physical parameters (distance, speed, acceleration, light, etc.)
   into electrical signals.
•  Perception: Understand the environmental state
•  Control: Enable closed-loop control for accuracy and stability.
•  Safety: Help the robot sense obstacles, navigate, and adapt to
   changing environments.
•  Learning: Feed data to AI/ML algorithms
•  Localization: Know where the robot is in space.
•  Manipulation: Grasp, push, pull with precision.
•  Sensors are the interface between the robot and the
   physical world


                                                                                                           4

visualInspection.notes: Transduction and all six roles viewed: perception, closed-loop control, safety, learning, localization, manipulation. Sensors provide evidence, not an automatic guarantee of stability or safety.

slides.title: Key Sensor Performance Characteristics
slides.text:
Key Sensor Performance Characteristics

•  Range: Minimum and maximum values the sensor can measure reliably.
•  Span: Maximum value – minimum value.
•   Error: measured value – true value.
•  Resolution: Smallest change in input that the sensor can detect.
•  Accuracy: Closeness of the measured value to the true value.
•  Precision: Repeatability — consistency of readings under the same conditions.
•  Dead Band: range of input values for which no output.
•  Dead Time: length of time from the application of an
   input until the output begins to respond to the change.
•  Sensor bandwidth (Hz): the range of frequencies
   over which a sensor can accurately measure and
   detect changes in a physical condition.



                                                                                                           6

visualInspection.notes: All definitions viewed: range endpoints; span=max-min; signed error=measured-true; resolution; accuracy; repeatability/precision; dead band; dead time; bandwidth Hz. Dead band wording no output is shorthand for no response/change, not necessarily zero signal. Distinguish bandwidth from sample/update rate and dead time from overall latency.

slides.title: •  Latency: the delay between a physical event and the availability of
slides.text:
•  Latency: the delay between a physical event and the availability of
   sensor output.
•  Sensitivity: Relationship indicating how much output one gets per unit
   input.
•  Hysteresis Error: Different output for the same value of the input,
   depending upon whether it has been obtained for an increasing value or
   for a decreasing value.
•  Linearity: Proportionality of output to input
   across the measurement range.
•  Noise: Random variation superimposed on the
   true signal value.



                                                                                                           7

visualInspection.notes: All five definitions viewed: latency, output-per-input sensitivity, direction-dependent hysteresis, linearity, random noise. Proportionality wording is a simplified linearity definition; an affine calibration may include offset. Distinguish bias, noise and hysteresis; sensitivity has output/input units.

slides.title: Potentiometer (Position Sensor)
slides.text:
Potentiometer (Position Sensor)

•  Definition
   – A potentiometer is an analog variable resistor used to measure angular or linear
        position.
•  Working Principle
   – A potentiometer has three terminals: Vcc, GND, and Wiper.
   – When the shaft rotates, the wiper moves along a resistive track.
   –  This changes the output voltage proportionally.
   – Arduino reads this voltage using its ADC (Analog to Digital Converter).
•  Applications in Robotics
   – Robotic arm joint angle sensing
   – Servo calibration
   – Manual control interfaces
   – Feedback in closed-loop systems      Rotary Potentiometer
                                            Source: https://www.build-electronic-circuits.com/

                                                                                                           8

visualInspection.notes: Every bullet and rotary component photo viewed. Three terminal divider uses supply, ground and wiper; linear track and negligible loading are needed for voltage proportional to position. ADC reads voltage, not angle without calibration. All four applications preserved.

Delay gives approximate maximum update rate ignoring overhead, not guaranteed exact sampling.

slides.title: Encoder (Rotary Encoder)
slides.text:
Encoder (Rotary Encoder)

•  Definition
   – An encoder converts mechanical motion
       into digital signals, allowing robots to
      measure speed, direction, and position.
•  Types                                                                Four bit
                                                                             absolute   – Incremental Encoder: Generates pulses per
                                                                      encoder
       revolution; needs a reference home
       position on startup; Common in servo
      motors
   – Absolute Encoder: Outputs a unique code
        for every shaft position; retains state after
       power-off; and is used in robotic arms.



                                                                                                          11

visualInspection.notes: Both diagrams inspected: optical transmitter/slotted disk/receiver; four concentric absolute tracks with sixteen binary labels 0000 through1111. Four-bit example is binary labeling, not automatically Gray code. Incremental pulses need reference for absolute position; single-turn absolute angle after power-up does not automatically preserve multi-turn history.

slides.title: Obstacle Avoidance Sensor (IR)
slides.text:
Obstacle Avoidance Sensor (IR)

•  Definition
   – An Infrared (IR) obstacle sensor detects objects by emitting infrared light and
       measuring the reflected radiation from nearby surfaces.
•  Working Principle
   –  IR LED emits infrared radiation.
   – Radiation strikes an obstacle.
   – Reflected IR is received by a photodiode or phototransistor.
   –  Signal strength changes based on distance.
   – Comparator converts analog signal into digital output.
•  Applications
   –  Line follower robots
   – Obstacle avoiding robots
   – Edge detection


                                                                                                          15

visualInspection.notes: All bullets and diagram rays viewed. IR LED sends light toward surface, photodiode receives reflection; intensity fed to comparator produces digital classification. Reflectivity/angle/ambient light affect signal as well as distance; digital threshold is not a calibrated range value. Three applications line-following, obstacle avoidance and edge detection.

    IR Sensor          Arduino Mega

   Vcc              5V

  GND           GND

   OUT              8
                                                               Source: https://circuitdigest.com/
•  Arduino Mega Code
      int irPin = 8;
     void setup() {                        Code Explanation
     pinMode(irPin, INPUT);
     Serial.begin(9600);            ― Digital output used
       }
     void loop() {                                    for decision-making
      int state = digitalRead(irPin);          ― High indicates
        if (state == HIGH) {Serial.println("Obstacle Detected"); }
     else {Serial.println("No Obstacle"); }                   obstacle presence
     delay(300);}


                                                                                                          16

visualInspection.notes: TableVcc5V/GND/OUT8; module photo labels VCC/GND/OUT and adjustable potentiometer. Code INPUT pin8,9600baud,digitalRead,stateHIGH prints Obstacle Detected else No Obstacle;delay300. Explicit active-high convention in code/prose must not be universalized to all module hardware.
